title: Episode 301: Edward I 'Longshanks': The Hammer of the Scots, the Conquest of Wales, and the Model Parliament
description:
The formidable, ruthless, and empire-building life of King Edward I, known to history as 'Longshanks' and the 'Hammer of the Scots': the towering six-foot-two warrior-king who conquered the principality of Wales, invaded Scotland, and created the permanent institutional structure of the English Parliament. Surviving captivity in the Barons' War and on Crusade in Acre, Edward crushed Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, erecting an invincible 'Iron Ring' of concentric stone castles across Wales—including Caernarfon, Conwy, and Harlech. Seizing the sacred Stone of Scone from Scotland, Edward confronted the rebellion of William Wallace and Robert the Bruce. Convening the historic Model Parliament of 1295 with the immortal doctrine 'what touches all should be approved by all', discover the Iron King.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series explores the titanic, terrifying, and brilliant monarch who conquered Wales, battled William Wallace for Scotland, and codified the laws and parliament of England. Here is George with the extraordinary life of Edward I Longshanks.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: LONGSHANKS: THE TALL PRINCE AND THE CRUSADE OF ACRE: 1239 TO 1274
Born in June 1239 at Westminster Palace, Edward was named by his devout father Henry III after Saint Edward the Confessor. Standing an astonishing six feet two inches tall in an era when average men were five feet six, with long muscular legs that earned him the nickname 'Longshanks', Edward was a natural athlete with a drooping left eyelid and an intimidating, piercing gaze. Having escaped captivity to destroy Simon de Montfort at Evesham in 1265, Edward joined the Ninth Crusade in 1270, sailing to Acre with his beloved wife Eleanor of Castile. While resting in his tent in June 1272, an Assassin sent by the Emir of Jaffa lunged with a poisoned dagger; Edward parried the thrust with his forearm, wrestled the assassin to the ground, and killed him with his own blade, surviving the venomous wound after an English surgeon sliced away the infected flesh. Learning of his father's death while traveling through Sicily, Edward returned to England in 1274 to be crowned king with magnificent celebrations.  Edward's formative youth was an intense baptism of fire: standing six feet two inches tall with broad shoulders and an iron constitution, he was an intimidating physical presence whose volcanic temper terrified courtiers, once shouting at an erring cleric with such ferocious volume that the poor priest collapsed and died of apoplexy on the spot. His experience on the Ninth Crusade in Acre in 1271 forged his cold, calculating military mindset: surviving the poisoned dagger of an Assassin through his own lightning reflexes and raw physical power, Edward witnessed the fanatical discipline of Islamic armies and the tactical value of concentric stone fortifications, returning to England in 1274 determined to establish absolute sovereign dominance across the British archipelago.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CONQUEST OF WALES AND THE DEATH OF LLYWELYN: 1277 TO 1283
Edward's supreme geopolitical vision was the total feudal mastery of the British Isles. When the native Prince of Wales, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, refused to pay homage to the English crown, Edward launched a massive, industrialized military campaign in 1277, deploying fifteen thousand troops, lumberjacks to clear mountain passes, and a fleet to seize the grain harvest of Anglesey, driving Llywelyn into the mountains of Snowdonia. When Llywelyn and his brother Dafydd revolted again in 1282, Edward struck with merciless finality: Llywelyn was killed in a skirmish near Builth, his severed head crowned with ivy and paraded through London on a lance before being displayed on the Tower of London. Dafydd was captured and subjected to a horrific new punishment designed specifically by Edward for high treason: he was dragged behind horses, hanged until nearly suffocated, disemboweled while alive, and his corpse cut into four quarters.  Edward's conquest of Wales was an industrialized military campaign executed with ruthless, modern efficiency: he mobilized thousands of English woodsmen to hack broad, fifty-yard-wide highways through the primeval Welsh oak forests of Snowdonia, while his navy seized the island of Anglesey to starve the Welsh mountaineers out of their high pastures. When Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed in an ambush near Builth in December 1282, Edward showed no chivalric mercy: he had the Prince of Wales's severed head crowned with a mock garland of silver ivy, displayed on the pillory at Cheapside, and mounted on the Tower of London to rot. His horrific execution of Llywelyn's brother Dafydd at Shrewsbury in 1283 established the barbaric ritual of hanging, drawing, and quartering as the permanent English penalty for high treason.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE IRON RING: CONWY, CAERNARFON, AND HARLECH: 1283 TO 1290
To hold Wales in permanent subjugation, Edward engineered the most ambitious military building program in European medieval history: the 'Iron Ring' of concentric stone castles. Commissioning master architect James of Saint George, Edward spent over eighty thousand pounds—nearly three years of royal income—constructing state-of-the-art fortresses at Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech, and Beaumaris. Engineered with concentric curtain walls, massive gatehouses, overlapping fields of arrow fire, and sea access for naval resupply, these fortresses were impregnable to native Welsh assaults. At Caernarfon Castle, built with polygonal towers and alternating bands of colored limestone evoking the Roman imperial walls of Constantinople, Edward presented his newborn infant son, Edward of Caernarfon, to the Welsh chieftains in 1284, promising them a native-born prince who spoke not a word of French or English—creating the title 'Prince of Wales'.  The 'Iron Ring' of concentric castles engineered by Edward I and master mason James of Saint George represented the pinnacle of medieval military architecture: costing over eighty thousand pounds, fortresses like Caernarfon, Conwy, and Harlech featured multiple concentric curtain walls, rounded flanking towers, deadly murder holes, and massive twin-towered gatehouses that could be defended by a handful of men against an army. At Caernarfon Castle, constructed with polygonal Romanesque towers designed to evoke the imperial eagle of Rome and the ancient Welsh legend of the Dream of Macsen Wledig, Edward presented his newborn infant son to the defeated Welsh lords in 1284, famously proclaiming him 'Prince of Wales', permanently annexing the principality to the English crown.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE ELEANOR CROSSES AND THE EXPULSION OF THE JEWS: 1290
In November 1290, Edward suffered the deepest personal tragedy of his life: his beloved wife Queen Eleanor of Castile, who had accompanied him on every campaign for thirty-six years, died near Lincoln. Heartbroken, Edward accompanied her funeral procession on the twelve-day journey to Westminster Abbey, ordering an ornate stone memorial cross erected at each of the twelve overnight stopping places—including Northampton, St. Albans, and Charing Cross—creating the immortal 'Eleanor Crosses'. However, that same year revealed the ruthless dark side of Edward's fiscal desperation: facing colossal debts from his Welsh castle building, Edward issued the Edict of Expulsion in July 1290, banishing all sixteen thousand Jewish residents from England, seizing their homes, properties, and outstanding debts to finance his royal treasury, an act of anti-Semitic persecution that stood for three hundred and fifty years.  The death of Queen Eleanor of Castile in November 1290 devastated Edward's emotional equilibrium: for thirty-six years, Eleanor had been his constant companion, following him to the Holy Land, Wales, and France, and bearing him sixteen children. The twelve magnificent Gothic 'Eleanor Crosses' erected at every stopping place of her funeral procession—from Lincoln to Charing Cross—were enduring testaments of royal love and stone masonry. Yet that same year revealed Edward's cold-blooded capacity for cruel political expediency: heavily indebted to Italian bankers and seeking a massive parliamentary subsidy, Edward issued the Edict of Expulsion in July 1290, banishing all sixteen thousand Jews from England, confiscating their homes and property, an act of anti-Semitic persecution that stripped the English realm of its Jewish community for three and a half centuries.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GREAT CAUSE AND THE STONE OF SCONE: 1291 TO 1296
When the seven-year-old Queen of Scots, Margaret the Maid of Norway, died mysteriously in 1290, Scotland was plunged into a succession crisis known as 'The Great Cause', with thirteen rival claimants competing for the crown. The Scottish nobility invited Edward to arbitrate the dispute; Edward accepted on the ruthless condition that all claimants first recognize him as supreme feudal overlord of Scotland. In 1292, Edward selected John Balliol as king, but immediately treated Balliol as a humiliated puppet, summoning the King of Scots to London like a common vassal. When Balliol rebelled and signed the 'Auld Alliance' with France in 1295, Edward marched north with a vengeance: he sacked Berwick in a bloody massacre, crushed the Scots at Dunbar, stripped Balliol of his royal robes, and seized the sacred Stone of Scone—the ancient coronation stone of Scottish kings—carrying it to Westminster Abbey to be encased in the English Coronation Chair.  Edward's intervention in the Scottish succession crisis of 1291 was a masterclass in predatory legal aggression: gathering the Scottish nobility on the banks of the Tweed at Norham, Edward refused to arbitrate the crown until every single Scottish earl and bishop acknowledged him as supreme feudal overlord of Scotland. When his puppet king John Balliol rebelled in 1296, Edward marched north with apocalyptic fury: his army stormed the wealthy port of Berwick-upon-Tweed, slaughtering over seven thousand Scottish men, women, and children in a three-day bloodbath until mills were turned by blood. Stripping Balliol of his royal tabard at Montrose, Edward seized the ancient Stone of Scone—the sacred coronation block of Celtic kings—and carried it to Westminster Abbey, declaring Scotland an annexed English province.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE MODEL PARLIAMENT: 1295
Facing simultaneous wars in France, Wales, and Scotland, Edward recognized that his colossal military expenditures required broad national consent to avoid the baronial revolts that had destroyed his father. In November 1295, Edward summoned the historic assembly celebrated as the 'Model Parliament' to Westminster. Drawing on ancient Roman legal doctrine, Edward's royal writ of summons articulated the immortal democratic maxim: 'Quod omnes tangit ab omnibus approbetur'—'That which touches all should be approved by all.' Summoning archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, barons, two knights from every shire, and two burgesses from every borough, Edward institutionalized the permanent two-chamber structure of Lords and Commons, cementing Parliament as the indispensable partner of the English Crown.  Facing simultaneous military emergencies in Scotland, Wales, and Gascony, Edward summoned the historic 'Model Parliament' in November 1295, establishing the permanent institutional architecture of representative government. Drawing on the Justinian legal code, Edward articulated the immortal constitutional principle: 'Quod omnes tangit ab omnibus approbetur'—that which touches the interests of all should be approved by all. By summoning not merely the great lords and bishops, but explicitly requiring the election of two knights from every shire and two citizens from every borough, Edward created the permanent bicameral structure of Lords and Commons, ensuring that the crown could only levy national taxation with the consent of the elected representatives of the people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE HAMMER OF THE SCOTS AND THE BURGH BY SANDS: 1297 TO 1307
Edward's final decade was an unyielding, bloody war against Scottish resistance: when William Wallace destroyed the English army at Stirling Bridge in 1297, Edward marched north, deploying Welsh longbowmen and heavy cavalry to crush Wallace at the Battle of Falkirk in 1298. In 1305, Wallace was captured and executed in London with barbaric cruelty. But in 1306, Robert the Bruce murdered his rival John Comyn and crowned himself King of Scots at Scone, reigniting the flame of Scottish independence. Enraged, elderly and crippled by severe dysentery, sixty-eight-year-old Edward rode north on horse litter for one final campaign. On July 7, 1307, within sight of the Scottish hills at Burgh by Sands on the Solway Firth, the great warrior breathed his last. Inscribed upon his plain grey marble tomb in Westminster Abbey stands the epitaph that captured his iron life: 'Edwardus Primus Scottorum Malleus Hic Est, 1308. Pactum Serva'—Here is Edward I, the Hammer of the Scots. Keep Faith.  Edward's final decade was an unyielding, bloody war against Scottish independence: when William Wallace rallied the common folk and annihilated the English army at Stirling Bridge in 1297, Edward personally led his longbowmen and cavalry to crush Wallace at Falkirk in 1298. Though Wallace was captured and barbarously executed in London in 1305, Robert the Bruce crowned himself King of Scots at Scone in 1306, defying the English colossus. Old, exhausted, and dying of dysentery on a horse litter, seventy-year-old King Edward rode north for one final invasion. Passing away on July 7, 1307, at Burgh by Sands on the Solway Firth, Edward asked that his bones be carried at the head of the English army until Scotland was subdued. King Edward I Longshanks was an iron sovereign of terrifying will, military genius, and legal mastery, who forged the institutions of Britain in stone and steel.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. King Edward I Longshanks forged Britain in stone and law, but left a fateful legacy to his son. Join us next week as Rebecca returns with the tragic reign of King Edward II, Piers Gaveston, the disaster of Bannockburn, and the She-Wolf of France. Until then, stay curious.
